prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B014 to B015. In round 1 I said B015 should win if the committee judged that clean attribution outweighs breadth of discovery, and the exchange has settled that for me. Every file, including those that rank B015 lower, calls it the best attributed and best confirmed candidate, and the chair's summary records that this is not disputed. The scientific case is stronger than I credited at the opening. The magic-wavelength condition removes the light shift for atoms held in a lattice, so many atoms can be interrogated at once in the Lamb-Dicke regime. That is a different architecture from the single-ion clocks honoured in 2012, and it is what turned optical clocks into instruments that test constants, relativistic geodesy and fundamental physics near 1e-18. Katori proposed the concept and built the first strontium lattice clock; Ye drove the accuracy frontier and the many-body understanding of the system. Their roles are separable and the two-name credit is compact. Agreement between laboratories and between species, which Pearce and Kroll point to, is independent confirmation of the kind B014 does not yet have outside IceCube. A citation worded around the lattice concept and its realisation, and not around combs or clocks in general, keeps it clear of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one I raised myself: B015 is a measurement capability and not a new phenomenon, and a committee that puts a new window on nature first could still reasonably prefer B014. The overlap with the frequency-comb prize of 2005 and the single-ion prize of 2012 is a real risk if the citation is loosely worded, and Ye's comb work belongs partly to that lineage. Two names leave out Lemonde at SYRTE, Lisdat at PTB, Ludlow, Lemke, Bloom, Hinkley and the single-ion groups, and nobody has shown that the cut is anything other than a judgement. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so a sceptic can call the application milestone premature. I think the last point is a matter of timing, decided by another body, and not a doubt about the science.

responses.point: The lattice clock is a different physical architecture from earlier optical clocks and is securely attributed and replicated at the 1e-18 level; the 2005 and 2012 overlap is answered by the magic-wavelength concept.
responses.response: You have persuaded me on the point where I was unsure in round 1. I asked whether the lattice idea is a separate achievement or an extension of work already recognised. Your answer, that many atoms at the magic wavelength in the Lamb-Dicke regime form a distinct architecture, is a physical difference and not a matter of wording, and it is why I now accept the citation can state the novelty. I do not retract that B014 is the larger discovery. I accept your point that I cannot call B014 mature at the prize level while its two-name credit and its independent confirmation outside IceCube are still open, and that is enough to move my first choice. Your disclosure of the stay in Hall's laboratory is background and not a tie to Ye; I would record it and not weight it.

responses.point: B014 has the greatest reach, but the two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, the AMANDA and DUMAND precursors and the people outside the credit make it less safe this year; he keeps it as first alternative.
responses.response: Your reasoning matches mine, and I note that you moved first, from the same first choice. We agree on the scientific ranking and differ on the configuration. I have to concede your point about credit: Halzen and Karle are defensible as conceiver and construction and analysis leader, but Kowalski, Klein, Waxman and the earlier pioneers would still be outside the prize, and I cannot give the committee a clean principle for that. I also agree that if B014 returns in a later year the citation should rest on the diffuse flux and not on the source associations, which are still statistically modest. I would not dismiss it. I would hold it as the leading alternative, and I would put it ahead of any quantum-computing part on novelty grounds.

responses.point: B018 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan) is the strongest condensed-matter case, but he concedes that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers cannot fit in three names, that the 2016 prize touches neighbouring ground, and that Xue's anomalous Hall work is left out.
responses.response: Your own case against shows why I keep B018 as an alternative and not as a first choice. The discovery is not in doubt and two decades of replication is ample maturity. The credit is the difficulty: Mele is the co-author of the founding Z2 papers, the HgTe proposers are absent, and the three-dimensional proposers are absent too. Whether the third name is Hasan or Xue is not settled by the files, and neither configuration is clean. I accept the chair's point that B015 has the least contested credit. If the committee turns to a topological prize I would want that choice made on the scientific record and not on the number of names.

responses.point: B015 is original and independently confirmed, a metrology prize can look less like a discovery of nature, and B030 is her second choice with an unsettled mechanism and experimental credit outside the three names.
responses.response: You answer my round-1 point fairly: instrument-driven advances begin many atomic-physics discoveries, and clock comparisons already yield bounds on constants. I accept that, and it is part of why I now support B015. On a two-part prize, I considered pairing B015 with B014 and rejected it. The three-person limit would force Halzen or Karle out, and that is exactly the credit split I think is hard to defend. On B030 I share your maturity concern, since the superconductivity mechanism is still debated and Cao is outside the credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate invention from the work honoured in 2005 and 2012, which depends on the citation wording more than on the physics.
Whether Katori and Ye can be defended against the claims of SYRTE, PTB, NIST and the single-ion groups; I have no third name that I think improves the credit.
Whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the second; I think it should not, but another member could weigh it differently.
Whether B014 would be the better prize if the committee decides that a new observational window outweighs attribution, and whether the credit could be settled by a different framing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not touch any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, Halzen, Karle or any other credited name. I have read Kroll's disclosure about Hall's laboratory and Johansson's WACQT roles and they do not change my own position.
